title: Hierarchical Structure in Attribute-Based Inner-Product Functional Encryption
abstract:
Attribute-based inner-product functional encryption (AB-IPFE), introduced by Abdalla et al. (Asiacrypt'20), is a cryptosystem that combines the access-control capability of attribute-based encryption (ABE) with the linear-computation capability of inner-product functional encryption. By introducing a hierarchical structure between these two functionalities, we can decompose the key generation algorithm into two steps. While such a structure has been extensively studied in contexts such as hierarchical IBE and delegatable ABE, it has received little attention in AB-IPFE despite its naturalness. 

In this paper, we formalize a framework for two-level hierarchies in AB-IPFE and classify existing schemes according to their hierarchizability. In particular, we focus on adaptively secure schemes that support expressive access control, such as arithmetic programs in the public-index setting and attribute-hiding inner-product predicates in the private-index setting. To the best of our knowledge, the only efficient constructions known to meet these requirements are those obtained from the framework of Abdalla et al. in the private-index setting and from the scheme of Datta and Pal (Asiacrypt'21) in the public-index setting. We propose several new pairing-based constructions that achieve adaptive security.

First, we revisit the approach of Abdalla et al. Based on their framework, we propose three types of constructions that trade off hierarchizability, ciphertext size, and secret-key size. These constructions are based on predicate encodings and therefore support arithmetic span programs or attribute-hiding inner-product predicates.

Second, we revisit the approach of Datta and Pal. Their scheme supports attribute-weighted sums, which differ slightly from our target functionality. Although this already yields an AB-IPFE scheme, the resulting scheme is limited to the non-zero-type key-policy setting. We efficiently adapt their scheme to obtain AB-IPFE schemes that also support zero-type predicates, and we propose a ciphertext-policy variant. All of the resulting constructions can be hierarchized, but their intermediate secret keys are large. We also propose variant schemes with shorter intermediate secret keys, at the cost of somewhat larger final secret keys. These schemes support arithmetic branching programs.

such as arithmetic programs in the public-index setting and attribute-hiding inner-product
predicates in the private-index setting. To the best of our knowledge, the only eﬃcient con-
structions known to meet these requirements are those obtained from the framework of Abdalla
et al. in the private-index setting and from the scheme of Datta and Pal (Asiacrypt’21) in
the public-index setting. We propose several new pairing-based constructions that achieve
adaptive security.

1     Introduction
Functional encryption (FE) [BSW11, O’N10] is a cryptosystem in which a user possessing a secret
key corresponding to a function f can recover only the partial information f (x) of the message
x from the ciphertext. However, functional encryption supporting arbitrary circuits still faces
challenges in terms of eﬃciency. Consequently, active research is underway to develop more eﬃcient
schemes by restricting the classes of functions supported. Among these, inner-product functional
encryption (IPFE) [ABDP15] is one of the most well-known schemes, specializing in vector inner-
product computations. The message takes the form of a d-dimensional vector x, and when the
ciphertext of x is decrypted using the secret key corresponding to a d-dimensional vector y, the
inner product ⟨x, y⟩ is obtained. In addition, encryption schemes with access control such as
identity-based encryption (IBE) and attribute-based encryption (ABE), which have been studied
for longer, can also be regarded as a type of FE with restricted functionality.
Attribute-based IPFE. In 2020, Abdalla et al. [ACGU20] proposed attribute-based inner-
product functional encryption (AB-IPFE) that supports functions that return inner product values
only when the attributes satisfy speciﬁc conditions. The message consists of a pair of an attribute
x̃ and a vector x, and the secret key is associated with a pair of an attribute ỹ and a vector y. If
x̃ and ỹ satisfy a speciﬁc relation R, ⟨x, y⟩ is obtained; otherwise, decryption fails. AB-IPFE is a
scheme that combines the capabilities of ABE and IPFE, but it cannot be constructed by simply
combining them. The constructions proposed by Abdalla et al. [ACGU20] are based on either
pairings or lattices. The pairing-based schemes can be broadly categorized into two types. The
ﬁrst is a transformation from predicate encoding [CGW15, Wee14], which achieves selective simu-
lation (SEL-SIM) security. The second is a transformation from functional encoding [ACGU20],
which achieves adaptive indistinguishability (AD-IND). The lattice-based schemes support only
identity-based access control. One is SEL-IND secure in the standard model, and the other is
AD-IND secure in the random oracle model.
    Following this work, Lai et al. [LLW21] proposed new lattice-based AB-IPFE schemes. By
introducing a new lattice sampling technique, they constructed an AD-IND secure identity-based
IPFE (IB-IPFE) and a SEL-IND secure collusion-bounded AB-IPFE, both of which are based
on the LWE assumption in the standard model. Nguyen et al. [NPP22] proposed a new AD-
IND secure key-policy AB-IPFE scheme and its extension to the multi-client setting by utilizing
dual pairing vector spaces. None of these schemes achieves both adaptive security and simulation
security. Edamura and Takayasu [ET25] proposed AD-SIM secure IB-IPFE constructions. In
addition, many extensions have been proposed, such as constructions in the multi-client/multi-
input setting [ATY23, DMPT25, NPP22, NPP25], the unbounded setting [CT26, DDM+ 23], the
decentralized setting [DP23, NPS25], and the registered setting [DPY24, ZZZ+ 25].
    Independently, Abdalla et al. [AGW20] proposed FE for attribute-weighted sums (AWS-FE),
which is closely related to AB-IPFE. In AWS-FE, the message consists of the public part x and
the private d-dimensional vector z. The secret key is associated with a function f that outputs a
d-dimensional vector. Decryption by skf returns the value of the inner product ⟨f (x), z⟩. Their
scheme was proved to be SEL-SIM secure. Later, Datta and Pal [DP21] proposed an AD-SIM
secure AWS-FE scheme.
Hierarchical FE. The hierarchical structure refers to the property that secret keys with weaker
authority can be derived from secret keys with stronger authority. It is used to distribute the burden
of key generation. Starting with the proposal of Hierarchical IBE (HIBE) in 2002 [GS02,HL02], the
hierarchical structure (i.e. delegatability) of encryption schemes has been studied for a long time.
It has been generalized to delegatable ABE [BGG+ 14, GVW15, GPSW06, LW11] and hierarchical
FE [ABG+ 13,BCG+ 17]. In delegatable ABE, the secret key skf ∧g can be derived from skf for any
pair of policies f, g. Similarly, in hierarchical FE, the secret key skg◦f can be derived from skf for
any pair of functions f, g.

    Another approach is based on arithmetic branching programs (ABPs). An adaptively secure
ABE scheme with ABP-based access control was introduced by Lin and Luo [LL20], and its core
technique was used in the AWS-FE scheme of Datta and Pal [DP21]. This AWS-FE scheme can
be used to obtain AB-IPFE, but its access-control capability is limited. In fact, it supports only
non-zero-type predicates, for which decryption is allowed if f (x̃) ̸= 0. This type of predicate
can be captured by an AWS-FE scheme capable of computing ⟨f (x̃) · y, x⟩, since we consider the
case where x̃ is public. However, zero-type predicates, for which decryption succeeds if f (x̃) = 0,
cannot be embedded into AWS-FE in such an eﬃcient way. On the other hand, Lin and Luo’s
ABE scheme supports both zero-type and non-zero-type predicates. In Section 6.1, by combining
these techniques, we construct an AD-SIM-secure AB-IPFE scheme that supports both types of
predicates in the key-policy setting. Although Lin and Luo’s ABE scheme is a key-policy scheme,
in Section 6.3, we also construct a ciphertext-policy AB-IPFE scheme using a similar technique.
    Our ABP-based constructions are hierarchizable and have compact ciphertexts and secret keys;
however, the attribute keys can be large. In fact, their size is quadratic in d. When d is much
larger than the other parameters, this may be undesirable. In Section 7.1, we propose variant
schemes whose attribute-key size is linear in d, at the cost of larger secret keys.

2.2    Functional Encryption
Functional encryption (FE) [BSW11] consists of the following four PPT algorithms. Let F denote
a set of functions that are deﬁned on the message space.

   • Setup(1λ ): Given a security parameter λ as input, it outputs a master public key mpk and a
     master secret key msk.
   • Enc(mpk, x): Given a master public key mpk and a message x as inputs, it outputs a ciphertext
     C.
   • KeyGen(msk, f ): Given a master secret key msk and a function f ∈ F , it outputs a secret
     key skf .

KeyGen and Dec also takes mpk as input, but we omit it from description for simplicity. This
scheme is called correct if the minimum value of

to be revealed from the ciphertext.
